title: Code as schema: how we generate the Increase API
summary: How Increase defines its API in application code and generates an OpenAPI schema, documentation, and SDKs from it, so the API can never drift from its implementation.
body_markdown:
The Increase API sits at the heart of our product and we want to make it great. For an API, greatness often lies in small details - are resources and fields named consistently? Does the API’s production behavior match its documentation? How helpful are the error messages? Are there language-specific SDKs available? Do they have strong types?


Holding a high quality bar as your API grows can be a ton of work, often requiring a dedicated team.[That’s not how we like to work](https://increase.com/articles/how-we-work) . We’ve instead invested lots of energy in an opinionated internal framework for API definition. It’s allowed a single engineer to own the developer experience (APIs, SDKs, documentation, etc) for all of Increase, even as our API has scaled to hundreds of endpoints. We think our framework is good and would like to extol its virtues to you.


## Application code is the source of truth


Every API method implements a common interface and must define an HTTP verb, path, parameter shape, and response shape. Here’s a simplified Account API (these examples are in Ruby, but you can write something similar in any language):


```text
class   AccountResource   <   APISchema  ::  AbstractResource
string   :  id  ,   documentation  :   "  The Account identifier  "
string   :  name  ,   documentation  :   "  The name of the Account  "
enum   :  funding  ,   documentation  :   "  The type of the Account  "  ,   cases  :   {
deposits  :   "  A depository account such as checking or savings  "  ,
loan  :   "  A loan account  "  ,
}
timestamp   :  created_at  ,   documentation  :   "  When the Account was created  "
end


class   AccountCreate   <   APISchema  ::  AbstractAPIMethod
signature   do
http_path   '  /accounts  '
http_verb   :  post
documentation   '  Create an Account  '
parameters   do
string   :  name  ,   documentation  :   AccountResource  .  attributes  .  name  .  documentation
enum   :  funding  ,
documentation  :   AccountResource  .  attributes  .  funding  .  documentation  ,
cases  :   AccountResource  .  attributes  .  funding  .  cases  ,
optional_with_default  :   :  deposits
end
returns   AccountResource
end


def   operate
account   =   Model  ::  Account  .  create!  (  name  :   params  .  name  ,   funding  :   params  .  funding  )
AccountResource  .  new  (
id  :   account  .  id  ,
created_at  :   account  .  created_at  ,
name  :   account  .  name  ,
funding  :   account  .  funding  ,
)
end
end
```


We try to create a “[pit of success](https://blog.codinghorror.com/falling-into-the-pit-of-success/) ” with the framework, both in defining the API shape and then working with it:


- Schema-definition methods are packed with assertions to enforce our API conventions. When possible these are checked at build time instead of runtime - not documenting your API method means it won’t typecheck. (Our Ruby code uses[Sorbet](http://sorbet.org/) for type checking, omitted here for clarity.)
- The framework handles parsing the raw HTTP request into a strongly typed Request object.
- We expose higher-level parameter and attribute types for common operations.


For example, if you now want to add a method to retrieve an Account, there’s a shorthand for parameters that are resource IDs. First, we associate` AccountResource` with the database model it should load automagically:


```text
class   AccountResource   <   APISchema  ::  AbstractResource
# ... attribute definitions from above
associated_model   Model  ::  Account
end
```


Then the GET method looks like:


```text
class   AccountRetrieve   <   APISchema  ::  AbstractAPIMethod
signature   do
http_path   '  /accounts/{account_id}  '
http_verb   :  get
documentation   '  Retrieve an Account  '
parameters   do
resource_id   :  account_id  ,
resource  :   AccountResource  ,
documentation  :   "  The ID of the Account to be retrieved  "
end
returns   AccountResource   # It's nice to be able to reuse these across different methods
end


def   operate
account   =   params  .  account   # the framework hands us a fully-hydrated Model::Account
AccountResource  .  from_model  (  account  )   # The associated_model call gives us a convenience method here now
end
end
```


Under the hood,` resource_id` safely loads the` Model::Account` with that ID and hydrates it into` params.account` . Our type system knows` params.account` is a` Model::Account` ,` params.funding` is an enum with exactly those two cases, and` AccountResource.new` takes an object that implements the attributes declared above.


We push as much validation into the framework as possible and try to keep each` operate` method thin. This gives us a lot of developer experience features for free. The framework can:


- Check for common typos, and give a better error message when possible (` Unknown parameter 'nmae' - did you mean 'name'?` )
- Check that you’re in the correct environment (` No Account exists with the ID 'account_123'. A similar object exists in the sandbox, are you in the correct environment?` )
- Check that you have the right permissions to access the resource
- Aggregate many “parse-time” errors together, so we can return a single error response with all of the mistakes in the request instead of a series of 400s.


Consistency and expressive errors help make a great API. Having an opinionated framework like this helps us keep those properties as we grow.


## From code to schema


Validation and API definition is only half of the framework’s job. The real magic is turning the code definition into a portable schema that can be used by tools in any language. For us, that is[OpenAPI 3.1](http://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0) , which has issues but is the least bad option we’ve found. Our API framework uses a big pile of Ruby reflection to translate our statically defined API shape into a[high-quality OpenAPI schema](http://increase.com/openapi.json) . (Some teams start by hand-writing an OpenAPI schema and code-generating server-side stubs for implementation. We think it’s impossible to maintain consistency and quality in a hand-written schema of this size.)


There’s an art to making a good OpenAPI schema, and the framework guides engineers toward success here too. Because we reuse` AccountResource` across multiple API methods, the OpenAPI generator extracts it into a` $ref` (and, in turn, code-generation tools consuming the spec would only define a single class for that shape). Generating the schema also lets us use advanced OpenAPI features like` discriminator` that would be impossible to encode by hand at our scale. We also generate extensions, such as per-case enum descriptions, for features that haven’t made it into the OpenAPI standard yet.


```text
components  :
schemas  :
account  :
title  :   Account
type  :   object
additionalProperties  :   false
properties  :
id  :
description  :   The Account identifier
type  :   string
name  :
description  :   The name of the Account
type  :   string
funding  :
description  :   The type of the Account
type  :   string
enum  :
-   deposits
-   loan
x-enum-descriptions  :
-   A depository account such as checking or savings
-   A loan account
created_at  :
description  :   When the Account was created
type  :   string
format  :   date-time
required  :
-   id
-   name
-   funding
-   created_at
```


OpenAPI also often gives you many ways to express the same thing (a rant post for another day). There are at least five ways to declare a nullable attribute in OpenAPI 3.1, each with trade-offs. Centralizing generation in one place lets us experiment with the format that’s best for our customers.


## From schema to everything else


An expressive, up-to-date schema document is probably the single most valuable thing you can hand to an agent building against your API. But we get a lot more! We use ours to build every other downstream API-related artifact we publish: our API reference,[language-specific SDKs](http://increase.com/documentation/software-development-kits) ,[Postman collections](http://postman.com/increaseapi) , etc. There are[lots](https://readme.com/)[of](https://redocly.com/)[tools](https://www.mintlify.com/) that can generate a nice documentation site from an OpenAPI schema but[we hand-roll ours](http://increase.com/documentation/api/accounts#account-object) so we can use long-tail features or extensions in the spec like` x-enum-descriptions` .


This means that the documentation of our API can’t drift from its implementation. It might sound basic but not every API has this property and it’s maddening to encounter ones that don’t.


## Putting it together


There are infinite ways to build and publish an API, but this is ours:


- Define a schema in code
- Centralize schema validation as much as possible
- Go “down” from the schema into strong types in your code
- Go “up” from the schema into an OpenAPI specification
- Go “up” from the specification into documentation, SDKs, etc


We’ve looked into open-sourcing our framework once or twice and stopped - it’s nice to have some coupling to the rest of our codebase (such as the` associated_model` method which ties it to our ORM). This code is well-suited for agents to write, though, so try pointing yours at this post and see where it gets you!
